turns.t: All right, Dana, the booking note says insulin review, and then in brackets, lows at night. Is that the headline?

That's the headline. Okay, so, you know I got that new sensor in the fall? The one that beeps? It woke my husband up before it woke me, which tells you something about how deeply I sleep through my own lows.
That's actually useful information. How often is it going off in the night?
About twice a week. Usually around three in the morning. I wake up drenched, my pajamas are soaked, and I have to go eat jelly beans in the dark like a raccoon.
Jelly beans at three a.m. Mm-hm. And is it a low every time the sensor beeps, or sometimes a false alarm?

Mostly real. The sensor says fifty-something, and my finger stick agrees, within a few points. Last Tuesday it said forty-four, and I just sat on the kitchen floor eating a banana, honestly feeling kind of silly.
Not silly. Anything else different lately, besides the nights?
I'm wiped out in the afternoons. Like around two, three o'clock I hit a wall. I thought it was the lows messing with my sleep, but maybe it's something else.
Could be both. Let me ask about some other things. Any blurry vision lately?
No, my eyes are fine, I had my eye exam last month, and they gave me the thumbs up.
Numbness or tingling in your feet?
No, nothing like that. My feet are the one part of me that behaves.
And any vomiting or stomach upset, because that can throw the sugars off.
Nope, no vomiting. Stomach's been good. Which is a relief, since I'm not allowed gluten anyway, so I'm cautious.
Right, the celiac. Let's make sure I have all your insulin and other medicines right. Walk me through a day.

So at bedtime, I take glargine, 20 units. Then with meals I take lispro, usually about 6 units, depending on what I'm eating and what the sensor says. And then lisinopril, 5 mg every morning, for the blood pressure.
And your other conditions, I have type 1 diabetes of course, high blood pressure, and celiac disease. Anything else?
That's the list. Oh, and my appendix came out when I was fifteen. It's in my chart somewhere, I think. Does that count?
It counts, we like complete records. Tell me about exercise, it matters for the nighttime lows.
I run three mornings a week, about five miles. And on Saturdays I have the 5K group, which is more of a social hour with some jogging.

There it is. Think of your body like a car in a cold garage. A hard run uses up the fuel in your muscles, and then overnight your body keeps pulling sugar in to refill the tank. If your long-acting insulin is still pushing hard at three a.m., you hit empty.
Oh. That actually explains why it happens after my Friday run and not after rest days.
Exactly. Okay, let me get your numbers. Arm out, please. Blood pressure is 122 over 76.
Pulse is 70, oxygen saturation is 99 percent, temperature 36.7, and you weigh 176 pounds on our scale.
Good, I was 180 at Thanksgiving, thanks to my mother-in-law's pie.
Those are all good. Here's what I think. The overnight lows look most likely like too much of the long-acting insulin at bedtime, particularly after exercise.
So I turn it down? I've been scared to touch it, honestly. Last time I changed a dose on my own, I overcorrected and went high for three days.
A small step, not a big one. I'd like you to cut the glargine from 20 units down to 18 units at bedtime, and keep everything else the same.
Eighteen. Okay. And if I still go low?
Then text the clinic, and we'll adjust again by another two. Meanwhile, have a small snack at bedtime on the days after you run.
A snack I'm allowed to have! Peanut butter on gluten-free toast, it is.
I also want a fresh HbA1c blood test before I see you, so we can see the longer picture.
I can do that on my way to work, the lab's right by my office.
Perfect. And I'd like to see you in three months to review how the nights are going.
Three months, okay. Thank you, doctor. I'll go home and tell my husband the jelly bean raccoon retires soon.
Let's hope. Take care, Dana.

Small snack at bedtime on days after running; text the clinic if lows continue
